body.objective: Students will be able to draw contour lines from observation.
body.iCan: I can draw contour lines from observation.
successCriteria: I can draw from observation instead of memory
I can use contour and blind contour lines
I can show the edges and details of natural forms
body.hook: Most people draw what they think a leaf looks like: a simple oval with a line down the middle. Artists draw what they actually see: the bumpy edge, the curling tip, the vein that splits in three. Contour drawing trains your eye to slow down and really look.

vocabulary.definition: Looking carefully at a real object while drawing it.
A line that follows the edges and important inner lines of a form.
Drawing an object's contour without looking at the paper.
Contour drawing where you glance at the paper only occasionally.
An object from nature, such as a shell, pine cone, leaf or feather.
How a line looks: thick or thin, light or dark, smooth or broken.

study.title: Seeing Edges
study.question: How does drawing from observation change what I see?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Warm-up, blind contour (3 × 2 minutes): Place a natural form (shell, pine cone, leaf, feather, seed pod) in front of you. Put your pencil on the paper and look only at the object. Move your eyes slowly along its edge and let the pencil follow at the same speed. Don't look down. The drawing will look strange; that's the point.
2. Modified contour (10 minutes): Draw the same object, glancing at the paper only to place your pencil. Include inner contours: veins, ridges, overlapping scales.
3. Line quality (10 minutes): Redraw one section larger. Use thick, dark lines for edges in shadow or closest to you and thin, light lines for edges in light or farther away.
4. Reflect: Compare your three drawings. What did you notice that you wouldn't have drawn from memory?

body.objective: Students will be able to show texture with mark-making.
body.iCan: I can show texture with mark-making.
successCriteria: I can create a range of marks to show texture
I can match marks to real textures in natural forms
I can use texture to make a drawing more realistic
body.hook: Close your eyes and run your fingers over tree bark, a feather and a smooth stone. Each feels completely different. Artists can't let you touch a drawing, so they use marks to make you feel the texture with your eyes.

vocabulary.definition: How a surface feels or looks like it would feel.
Texture that is drawn or painted to look real.
Using different lines, dots and strokes to create effects.
Using many small dots to create texture or shading.
Using crossing sets of lines to create texture or shading.

study.title: Texture Library
study.question: How can marks make a drawing look rough, smooth or soft?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Texture library (15 minutes): Divide a page into 12 boxes. Fill each with a different kind of mark: dots (stippling), short dashes, long parallel lines (hatching), crossing lines (cross-hatching), scribbles, circles, wavy lines, zigzags, smudges with a finger, eraser lines through graphite, dense dark marks, very light marks. Label each with a texture it could show (bark, fur, water, sand).
2. Texture hunt (10 minutes): Examine three natural forms closely (a feather, bark, a rock, a pine cone). For each, choose the marks from your library that match.
3. Texture drawing (25 minutes): Draw a contour of one natural form, then fill it with implied texture using your chosen marks. Make dark areas with denser marks and light areas with fewer.

body.objective: Students will be able to use value to create form.
body.iCan: I can use value to create form.
successCriteria: I can create a value scale
I can identify highlight, mid-tone, core shadow and cast shadow
I can use value to show form in a drawing
body.hook: Draw a circle and it's flat. Add shading from light to dark, and suddenly it's a ball you could pick up. Value, the lightness and darkness of a surface, is the trick artists use to make flat paper look three-dimensional.

vocabulary.definition: How light or dark something is.
A row of boxes showing a range from white to black.
The lightest area, where light hits most directly.
The darkest part of the shadow on the object itself.
The shadow an object throws onto the surface behind or below it.
A three-dimensional shape with height, width and depth.

study.title: Light and Shadow
study.question: How does value turn shapes into forms?
study.passage:
Studio steps (written for this lesson):
1. Value scale (10 minutes): Draw a row of seven boxes. Leave the first white. Shade each box a little darker until the last is as dark as your pencil can go. Use a 2B or 4B pencil and build up layers rather than pressing hard at once.
2. Sphere study (15 minutes): Shine a lamp on a white ball from one side. Draw a circle. Find and shade: the highlight (lightest, nearest the light), the mid-tones, the core shadow (darkest band on the ball, away from the light), reflected light (a slightly lighter edge inside the shadow) and the cast shadow on the table.
3. Natural form (25 minutes): Light a natural form (shell, gourd, egg, pine cone) from one side. Draw its contour, then shade it with at least five values from your scale.
Tip: squint at the object. Squinting hides details and shows the big light and dark shapes.
